name: Alkaline
self_discharge: About 3% of capacity per year stored at 20 °C (Energizer, cylindrical cells)
summary: Alkaline cells, also called alkaline manganese dioxide cells, pair a zinc anode with a manganese dioxide cathode in a potassium hydroxide electrolyte and deliver 1.5 V nominal on a sloping discharge curve. They are the default single-use chemistry for AA, AAA, C, D and 9 V batteries.
body:
## How it works

An alkaline cell pairs a zinc anode with a manganese dioxide cathode in an aqueous potassium hydroxide electrolyte. Energizer's handbook describes the usual cylindrical construction: high-density manganese dioxide lines the inside of a steel can, which serves as the cathode current collector, and a gelled zinc powder anode fills the center, contacted by a brass collector. A nylon seal closes the cell and also acts as a vent. The overall reaction Energizer gives is Zn + 2MnO2 + H2O → ZnO + 2MnOOH. Hydrogen gas is a byproduct of the chemistry in all alkaline cells.

## Discharge behavior

The discharge curve slopes. With no load, a fresh cell reads 1.50 to 1.65 V depending on the purity of the manganese dioxide, and the closed-circuit voltage falls steadily as capacity is used. Energizer recommends 0.8 V per cell as the minimum cutoff, because deeper discharge raises the chance of excessive internal gassing; by 0.8 V about 95% of the usable capacity has been removed.

Delivered capacity depends on load and on the device's cutoff. In Energizer's AA (LR6) example, the same cell gives about 2500 mAh at 100 mA to 0.8 V but about 1500 mAh to 1.2 V. Fresh cylindrical cells show an effective internal resistance of roughly 150 to 300 mΩ, depending on size, measured with a 505 mA, 100 ms pulse. Energizer rates operation from −18 to 55 °C and storage from −40 to 50 °C, and states that cylindrical cells lose about 3% of capacity per year at 20 °C.

## Uses

Alkaline is the common single-use chemistry for household round cells, sold under IEC designations such as LR6 (AA), LR03 (AAA), LR14 (C), LR20 (D) and 6LR61 (9 V), and for LR button cells. Wikipedia reports that as of 2011 alkaline batteries accounted for 80% of batteries manufactured in the United States.

## History

Lewis Urry, Karl Kordesch and P. A. Marsal of Union Carbide filed for US patent 2,960,558 on an alkaline dry cell in 1957; it was granted in 1960. Energizer dates the commercial introduction of the alkaline manganese dioxide cell to 1959. Early cells used zinc amalgamated with mercury to suppress side reactions. Manufacturers moved to purer zinc, and EU law (Directive 2006/66/EC as amended by 2013/56/EU) limits mercury in any battery to 0.0005% by weight.

## Status

Current. IEC 60086-1 assigns the system letter L: zinc negative electrode, alkali metal hydroxide electrolyte, manganese dioxide positive electrode, 1.5 V nominal and 1.65 V maximum open-circuit voltage.
strengths: Higher energy density than carbon zinc
Better service than carbon zinc at all drain rates (Energizer)
Long shelf life: about 3% capacity loss per year at 20 °C
Widely available in every common household size
limitations: Sloping voltage: capacity depends heavily on the device cutoff
Capacity falls sharply at high drain and low temperature
safety: Produces hydrogen gas; in sealed or waterproof devices the gas can accumulate and mix with air to form an explosive atmosphere
Abuse such as charging or short-circuiting raises hydrogen generation
Attempting to recharge can cause rupture or leakage
Loose cells mixed together can short-circuit each other, particularly button cells
